content.text:
Start working on Linear ticket obsidian-ai-tutorial. this is not an official Linear ticket. but i want to start a worktree to do some experimental work. here is the general direction:

* growth engineer project: help people onboard on Obsidian vault easier
* how: we used to have some scaffolding for Obsidian tutorial using overlays to guide steps to do xyz at some point. i can't remember what branch it is anymore or whether it still exists locally or remotely on Github. but i want to use some of this to build this feature: have user input in a use case they want to do with Obsidian -> generate the tutorial for them to follow through
* feel free to /grill by fetching its details and creating a dedicated git worktree.

## Steps

### 1. Validate input
- `obsidian-ai-tutorial. this is not an official Linear ticket. but i want to start a worktree to do some experimental work. here is the general direction:

* growth engineer project: help people onboard on Obsidian vault easier
* how: we used to have some scaffolding for Obsidian tutorial using overlays to guide steps to do xyz at some point. i can't remember what branch it is anymore or whether it still exists locally or remotely on Github. but i want to use some of this to build this feature: have user input in a use case they want to do with Obsidian -> generate the tutorial for them to follow through
* feel free to /grill` should be a Linear ticket ID like `ENG-1271`. If missing or malformed, ask the user.

### 2. Fetch ticket details from Linear
- Use `mcp__linear-server__get_issue` with the issue ID `obsidian-ai-tutorial. this is not an official Linear ticket. but i want to start a worktree to do some experimental work. here is the general direction:

* growth engineer project: help people onboard on Obsidian vault easier
* how: we used to have some scaffolding for Obsidian tutorial using overlays to guide steps to do xyz at some point. i can't remember what branch it is anymore or whether it still exists locally or remotely on Github. but i want to use some of this to build this feature: have user input in a use case they want to do with Obsidian -> generate the tutorial for them to follow through
* feel free to /grill`
- Extract: title, description, and `branchName` (Linear provides this)
- If the Linear tool is unavailable, ask the user for a branch name manually

### 3. Determine branch name
- Use the `branchName` field from Linear if available (it's already formatted correctly)
- Otherwise derive it: lowercase the ticket ID + hyphenated slug of the title
  - Example: `ENG-1271 Implement filter search` → `eng-1271-implement-filter-search`
  - Strip special characters, replace spaces with hyphens, truncate to ~60 chars

### 4. Create git worktree
Run these from the repo root (the main working directory, not an existing worktree):

```bash
# Fetch latest main so the worktree starts from up-to-date origin/main
git fetch origin main

# Check if branch already exists
git branch --list <branch-name>

# Check if worktree already exists
git worktree list | grep <branch-name>
```

- **If worktree already exists**: skip to step 5, just `cd` into `.claude/worktrees/<branch-name>`
- **If branch does NOT exist**: `git worktree add -b <branch-name> .claude/worktrees/<branch-name> origin/main`
- **If branch already exists but no worktree**: reset the branch to `origin/main` first, then add the worktree:
  ```bash
  git branch -f <branch-name> origin/main
  git worktree add .claude/worktrees/<branch-name> <branch-name>
  ```

### 5. Enter the worktree
**Do NOT use the `EnterWorktree` tool** — it always creates a brand-new worktree and will duplicate the one you just created.

Instead, use `cd` to switch into the worktree directory:
```bash
cd .claude/worktrees/<branch-name>
```

All subsequent commands should run from this path.

### 6. Install dependencies and set up the worktree
After entering the worktree, run the following to bootstrap the environment:

```bash
pnpm install
```

This is required because worktrees share git objects but each needs its own `node_modules`.

### 6b. Copy .env files from the main repo into the worktree
`.env` files are gitignored, so each worktree needs its own copies. After `pnpm install`, copy all `.env` files (excluding `.env.example` files) from the main repo root into the matching relative paths in the worktree.

The main repo root is the working directory you were in before entering the worktree (e.g. `/Users/trang.doan/Desktop/code/discourse-graph`).

Run:
```bash
# From the main repo root, find all .env files (not .env.example) and copy them into the worktree
find . -name ".env*" \
  -not -name ".env.example" \
  -not -path "./.git/*" \
  -not -path "./node_modules/*" \
  -not -path "./.claude/worktrees/*" \
  | while read f; do
      dest=".claude/worktrees/<branch-name>/$f"
      mkdir -p "$(dirname "$dest")"
      cp "$f" "$dest"
    done
```

Report which files were copied so the user can confirm.

The copied `OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_PATH` points at the main checkout's vault. Step 7 replaces it
with the vault leased to this worktree.

### 6c. Link the shared `dg-*` skills into the worktree

Claude Code only loads skills from `.claude/skills`, but the repo's shared skills live in
`.agents/skills`. Without this step they never load in the worktree: they cannot trigger on
their own descriptions and have no slash command.

Run from the main repo root, substituting the worktree path:

```bash
WT=".claude/worktrees/<branch-name>"
MAIN="$PWD"
mkdir -p "$WT/.claude/skills"
for src in "$MAIN"/.agents/skills/dg-*/; do
  s=$(basename "$src")
  if [ -d "$WT/.agents/skills/$s" ]; then
    # Relative link, so the worktree uses its own branch's copy of the skill.
    ln -sfn "../../.agents/skills/$s" "$WT/.claude/skills/$s"
  else
    # Branch predates the skill; fall back to the main checkout's copy.
    ln -sfn "$MAIN/.agents/skills/$s" "$WT/.claude/skills/$s"
  fi
done
ls -l "$WT/.claude/skills/"
```

Verify each link resolves before moving on:

```bash
for d in "$WT"/.claude/skills/dg-*; do
  [ -f "$d/SKILL.md" ] || echo "BROKEN: $d"
done
```

These links are gitignored (`.claude/*`), so they are local to this machine and add nothing
to the diff. Use a glob rather than a variable list: zsh does not word-split unquoted
variables, so `for s in $SKILLS` silently iterates once with the whole string.

### 7. Ask the user which app to start
Ask the user which app they want to run in dev mode. Common options:
- **Roam**: `SUPABASE_USE_DB=none pnpm -C <worktree>/apps/roam dev`
- **Obsidian**: `node ~/.claude/skills/obsidian-vault/scripts/vault.mjs dev --worktree <worktree>`
  - This leases a free local-db vault and writes `OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_PATH` and `SUPABASE_USE_DB` for
    it into `<worktree>/apps/obsidian/.env`. It then starts the watcher. A later plain `pnpm dev`
    and CDP runs use the same vault. Add `--db production` only if the user asks to test against
    prod (testVault123).
  - For **None**, still run `vault.mjs claim --worktree <worktree>` if the ticket touches
    apps/obsidian, so the `.env` doesn't keep pointing at the main checkout's vault.
  - **Exit 2** means every vault in that pool is taken. Follow the `obsidian-vault` skill: ask the
    user which vault to take over, then rerun with `--take <vault>`. Never pick one yourself.
  - On success, pass the printed `obsidian://open?path=` URL to the user, so they open that vault.
- **None**: just set up the environment without starting a dev server

If the user says Roam, also switch the Roam dev symlink:
```bash
ln -sfn <worktree>/apps/roam/dist ~/roam-ext-dev
```
and remind them to reload the developer extension in Roam.

Run the chosen dev command in the background so the user can continue working.

**Dev server gotchas** (learned the hard way — don't rediscover these):

- The filter flag is `--filter`, not `--F`. Turbo 2.5.6 rejects `--F=roam` outright.
- Prefer `pnpm -C <abs-path> <app> dev` over `turbo dev --filter=<app>`. `turbo dev --filter=roam`
  also runs the `@repo/database#dev` dependency, which requires Docker Desktop plus an explicit
  `SUPABASE_USE_DB`; if Docker isn't running turbo fails the *entire* run even though the app
  itself built fine. Going through `pnpm -C` skips the dependency graph.
- `SUPABASE_USE_DB` must be one of `local | branch | production | none | implicit`
  (see `packages/database/src/dbDotEnv.mjs`). Use `none` for work that doesn't touch the database.
- **Always bake the absolute worktree path into the command.** The Bash tool's cwd resets to the
  main repo between calls, so a backgrounded `pnpm --filter roam dev` with no path silently builds
  the *main repo's* `dist` — not the worktree the symlink points at. `pnpm -C <abs-path>` makes the
  path intrinsic to the command so it can't be dropped.
- After starting, verify before reporting success: confirm the log says `built with 0 errors` **and**
  that `<worktree>/apps/roam/dist` has a fresh mtime. A background task that failed still returns a
  task ID.

### 8. Ingest any saved session context
The branch may have been worked on before (e.g. reset from an existing branch).
Check for recorded session context:

```bash
bash ~/.claude/scripts/session-context.sh resolve
```

- If `CONTEXT_EXISTS=yes`, **read the `CONTEXT_FILE`** and load it as working context
  (`Next step`, `Open questions`, `Key decisions`, `Dead ends`).
- If `CONTEXT_EXISTS=no` or the command errors, continue — this is a fresh start.

### 9. Show context
After setup, display:
- Ticket ID and title
- Branch name you're on
- Brief description from the ticket (if available)
- Which app dev server is running (if any), and for Obsidian, which vault is leased
- That the shared `dg-*` skills are linked and resolving
- If prior session context was found: its `TL;DR` and `Next step`
- A short "ready to work" confirmation
- Remind the user they can run `/checkpoint` to save session context before wrapping up
No Linear ticket here, so I'll use `obsidian-ai-tutorial` as the branch name. I'll set up the worktree, and a background agent will look for the old overlay tutorial scaffolding at the same time.

I found the old work: it's on remote branch `origin/eng-1505-timebox-to-create-skeleton-for-onboarding-user-flow`.

## Ready to work

- **Ticket:** `obsidian-ai-tutorial`, experimental. There's no Linear ticket.
- **Branch and worktree:** `obsidian-ai-tutorial` in `.claude/worktrees/obsidian-ai-tutorial`, created from `origin/main` at `7523cc8c`.
- **Dependencies and env:** installed, and the `.env` files were copied over. That includes `apps/obsidian/.env`, `.env.branch` and `.env.bak-eng2114`, plus files in `apps/roam`, `apps/website`, `packages/database` and `skills/`.
- **Skills:** all 8 shared `dg-*` skills are linked and load.
- **Obsidian:**
  - The watcher is running and built with 0 errors into **testVault**, using the local database.
  - I took testVault over from eng-2363, which wasn't running anything on it.
  - Open the vault with `obsidian://open?path=%2FUsers%2Ftrang.doan%2FDocuments%2FtestVault`.
- **Saved session context:** none, so this is a fresh start.

## The old overlay tutorial

- **Where it is:** one work-in-progress commit, `c1f4e258` from 2026-03-31, made for ENG-1505 ("timebox to create skeleton for onboarding user flow"). It was never opened as a PR and isn't on main.
- **What it does:** it has two versions of the same 3-step tour. The tour goes: click the telescope ribbon icon, press Cmd+P, then type "Create discourse node".
  - **A. Custom React overlay** (`apps/obsidian/src/components/onboarding/`):
    - Each step is plain data: a target element, a title, a description, and how the step finishes (on a click, or when an element appears).
    - A spotlight dims the rest of the screen, and clicks still go through to the real Obsidian UI.
    - It runs from a "Start onboarding tour" command.
  - **B. driver.js version:** each phase is written out step by step in code, with a 307-line stylesheet.
- **What to reuse:** A is the better base. Steps are just data, which is the form a "generate a tutorial from the user's use case" feature would need to output.
- **What's missing:**
  - It doesn't save progress.
  - It never checks that the user actually did the step.
  - It doesn't clean up its listeners when the plugin unloads.
  - It re-checks the target's position on every frame.

content.text:
These five decisions don't depend on anything else, so they're all up for answer now.

❓ **Q1** - **Who is the user?** Who do you most want this to unblock?
- (a) Someone new to Obsidian who installed Discourse Graphs because a lab or collaborator told them to.
- (b) An experienced Obsidian user who is new to Discourse Graphs.
- (c) Both, with the tutorial adapting to what they already know.

➡️ Go with (a). The onboarding gap is widest for them, and it's the growth segment. Experienced users can read the docs. A single target user also keeps the experiment's results easy to read.

---

❓ **Q2** - **How much can a tutorial cover?**
- (a) Only Discourse Graphs features: node types, creating nodes, relations, the discourse context panel, the canvas.
- (b) Discourse Graphs plus the core Obsidian skills it relies on: the command palette, links, the file explorer, properties.
- (c) Anything you can do in Obsidian, such as daily notes, templates, or other plugins.

➡️ Go with (b). A new Obsidian user can't use Discourse Graphs without the basics. With (c), the AI would be guiding people through UI we don't control and can't test.

---

❓ **Q3** - **What is this experiment meant to produce?**
- (a) A throwaway prototype that answers "do people want this, and does generation work?", shown as a demo or to a few users.
- (b) A first version that can ship behind an experimental setting to real users.
- (c) A design or spec only, with no code.

➡️ Go with (a) to start, and plan for (b) next. Building a prototype first is cheap and shows whether AI-generated tours are reliable enough before anyone polishes the overlay.

---

❓ **Q4** - **How much does the AI make up?** This is the decision that matters most.
- (a) **Free-form.** The model writes whole steps, including the screen element each step points at and the condition that moves to the next step. It's flexible, but it will invent elements that don't exist and steps that never finish.
- (b) **Assembled from a library.** We write and test a set of step building blocks, such as `open-command-palette`, `create-node(type)`, `add-relation`, `open-discourse-context` and `link-notes`. Each block has known screen targets and completion checks. The model only picks blocks, puts them in order, fills in values, and writes the explanation text for the user's use case.
- (c) **Hybrid.** Use library blocks wherever possible, and allow a free-text "do this yourself" step when no block fits.

➡️ Go with (c), which is (b) with a fallback. Every on-screen highlight stays reliable because each one is a block we've tested, while the AI still decides what the tutorial covers and how to word it. The step format from eng-1505 already suits library blocks.

---

❓ **Q5** - **Where does the user enter their use case?**
- (a) A welcome window on first launch after install, with a prompt like "What do you want to use your vault for?".
- (b) A command, "Generate a tutorial for…", available any time.
- (c) Both.

➡️ Go with (c), but build (b) first, since a command is the cheapest to make and test. Then add (a) because first launch is when it matters for growth. The old branch's first-launch notice can lead into it.

---

The next round covers where the AI runs, privacy, and how to measure success. It's waiting on a background lookup of our existing AI and analytics setup, which is still running.

## Q4 explained

The deciding fact is that **the model doesn't see our codebase when it runs.** When a user types "I want to track claims from papers I read", the plugin sends one request to the AI service. The model only knows what's written in that request plus what it learned in general training. Training gives it a rough idea of Obsidian and almost nothing about Discourse Graphs' interface. So it has to guess the exact screen element to point at, and it guesses wrong.

Here's how each step works in the overlay. A step needs two things to be precise:

1. **Where to point.** That's an exact handle on a screen element, such as `.side-dock-ribbon-action[aria-label="Toggle discourse context"]`.
2. **When the step is done.** That's a check like "the command palette opened" or "a note with a Claim node type now exists".

If either is wrong, the spotlight lands on nothing or the tutorial gets stuck. These handles also change between Obsidian versions. For example, in Obsidian 1.13 Settings became a separate window.

Take the use case "track claims from papers". The two approaches produce different output:

**(a) Free-form.** The model writes each step itself.
```
{ target: ".dg-create-claim-btn",        ← invented, doesn't exist
  title: "Click Create Claim",
  doneWhen: "click on .dg-create-claim-btn" }
```

**(b) Library blocks.** We write and test these once:
```
create-node(type)        → knows the real command, real target, and checks the node file exists
open-discourse-context   → knows the ribbon icon and checks the panel opened
add-relation(from, to)   → ...
```
The model only picks the blocks and writes the wording:
```
1. create-node("Source")   "First, add the paper you're reading as a Source"
2. create-node("Claim")    "Now write one claim it makes"
3. add-relation(...)       "Link the claim to the paper so you can trace it later"
```

Your instinct that "the model understands our codebase" is right, but it applies **when we build the blocks, not when the user runs the tutorial.** Claude Code, with access to the repo, can write most of the blocks: read the code, find the real targets, write the done-checks. We then check each block in real Obsidian once. Every user prompt after that only needs the model to arrange blocks, which it's reliable at.

So yes, blocks are reusable steps, but each one is tested. The value of reusing them is that they're tested; saving effort is secondary.

## Round 2

❓ **Q4 (again)** - **Which approach?** Now that the tradeoff is clearer:
- (a) The model writes whole steps.
- (b) The model only picks from tested blocks.
- (c) Blocks wherever possible. When no block fits, the model writes a text-only step with no spotlight and a "Done" button the user clicks.

➡️ Go with (c). There's also a cheap way to test this: run 10 real prompts through a free-form prototype first and count how many steps point at the wrong element. That's an afternoon of work and gives us data instead of opinions.

---

❓ **Q2** - **How much can a tutorial cover?** (still open)
- (a) Discourse Graphs only.
- (b) Discourse Graphs plus the core Obsidian basics it needs.
- (c) Anything in Obsidian.

➡️ Go with (b). Your answer to Q1 includes people new to Obsidian, so the basics are needed. Choosing (c) would mean writing blocks for other people's plugins.

---

❓ **Q5** - **Where does the user enter the prompt?** (still open)
- (a) A welcome window on first launch.
- (b) A command.
- (c) Both.

➡️ Go with (c), building (b) first for the prototype.

---

❓ **Q6** - **How does the tutorial adapt to someone who already knows Obsidian?** This follows from your Q1 answer.
- (a) Ask one question before generating, such as "New to Obsidian?", and have it skip or include the basics blocks.
- (b) Infer it from the vault: how many notes it has, other plugins installed, whether it has existing links.
- (c) Always include the basics, with a "Skip, I know this" button on each of those steps.

➡️ Go with (a) and add the per-step skip from (c). It's explicit and costs one click. Inferring from the vault (b) reads the user's data and is easy to get wrong.

---

❓ **Q7** - **Which AI path does the prototype use?**
- (a) The existing website endpoint, `/api/llm/anthropic/chat`, which already allows requests from Obsidian. The response comes back as a structured list of steps.
- (b) Users supply their own API key.
- (c) A new endpoint just for tutorials.

➡️ Go with (a) for the prototype, since it needs no setup. Before anything ships to real users, that endpoint needs rate limiting. I'll note it as a blocker for shipping, not for the prototype.

---

❓ **Q8** - **How does the prototype prove it works?** The Obsidian plugin has no analytics.
- (a) Watch 3–5 people try it, both new users and Obsidian users, and note where they get stuck.
- (b) Add analytics now, for things like tutorial started, each step completed, and abandoned.
- (c) A self-check: run a fixed set of about 20 use-case prompts and score whether every generated tutorial can be completed.

➡️ Go with (c) plus (a). Option (c) measures whether the tutorials work at all, and (a) measures whether they actually help people. Analytics (b) belongs with shipping later, and it would be a separate project because Obsidian has none.

Q4:c, but maybe in real time we could also have the model read our docs (that's publicly available instead of having to read code) to generate steps? because while we can build blocks it's not necessarily the same steps everywhere
agree with the rest of your recommendations

Settled: **Q2 (b), Q4 (c) with docs added, Q5 (c) with the command first, Q6 (a) plus a per-step skip, Q7 (a), Q8 (c) plus (a).**

Using the docs is a good addition, with one limit. Docs say *what* to do and in what order, for example "create a Claim, then link it to its Source". That's exactly what the model needs to pick blocks and order them sensibly. But docs describe the screen in words, like "click the telescope icon", not as an exact element handle. So when a step comes from the docs alone, it can explain but can't spotlight.

Your point that steps aren't always the same suggests a middle tier. Some handles can be read **from the running app itself**, and these are reliable:

- the list of real commands (each has a fixed ID)
- the ribbon icons (their hover labels)
- the settings tabs

That gives three tiers:

1. **Tested blocks:** a spotlight plus a precise done-check.
2. **General blocks checked against the live app:**
   - `run-command(id)`: the model can only choose IDs from the actual command list, and the step is done when that command runs.
   - `click-ribbon(label)`: done when the icon is clicked.
   - `open-settings-tab(id)`: done when that tab opens.

   These cover many flows that differ between setups, with no extra blocks to write.
3. **Text-only steps written from the docs:** no spotlight, and the user clicks "Done".

I'm also sending an agent to find where the docs live and how big they are. That decides whether we can send all of them with each request or need to pick the relevant pages, which belongs to the next round.

## Round 3

❓ **Q9** - **Add the middle tier?** These are the general blocks checked against the live app: `run-command`, `click-ribbon`, `open-settings-tab`.
- (a) Yes, with all three tiers: tested blocks, general blocks checked against the live app, and text-only steps.
- (b) No, only tested blocks and text-only steps.

➡️ Go with (a). It's the tier that handles your point that steps aren't always the same, and it's cheap because we read the lists from the live app rather than writing a block per flow.

---

❓ **Q10** - **Which version of the docs does the model read?**
- (a) Fetch them live from the website each time a tutorial is generated.
- (b) Bundle the docs into the plugin at build time.

➡️ Go with (b). The docs then always match the plugin version the user has installed. Live docs can describe a feature their version doesn't have yet. Bundling also saves a network request and keeps the docs and the code changing together.

---

❓ **Q11** - **What does the model learn about the user's vault?** Users can rename or add node and relation types, so `create-node("Claim")` only works if "Claim" exists in their vault.
- (a) Only their prompt.
- (b) Their prompt plus the vault's Discourse Graphs setup: node type names, relation type names, and the live command list. Never note titles or note contents.
- (c) Their prompt plus some notes, for more personal examples.

➡️ Go with (b). The model needs the real type names to fill in blocks correctly, and none of that is private. Option (c) would send research notes to a third party, so it should be a deliberate later decision, not a default.

---

❓ **Q12** - **Real notes or practice notes?** Tutorial steps create notes.
- (a) Real notes in the vault, wherever the user's settings put them.
- (b) Practice notes in a `Tutorial/` folder, with an option at the end to keep them or delete them.
- (c) A separate practice vault.

➡️ Go with (a), plus an end-of-tutorial screen that lists what was created and lets the user delete it. The prompt is the user's real goal, so the notes are the start of their real work. A practice folder teaches a different flow from the one they'll actually use.

---

❓ **Q13** - **What happens when a step can't be completed?** The target element may be missing, the user may do something else, or the done-check may never pass.
- (a) Show the step as a text-only card with "Skip", "Mark done" and "I'm stuck". "I'm stuck" sends the remaining steps plus what's on screen now back to the model to rewrite the rest of the tutorial.
- (b) Only "Skip" and "Quit".

➡️ Go with (a), but leave "I'm stuck → rewrite" out of the first prototype. The 20-prompt self-check will show whether stuck steps happen often enough to justify it.

---

❓ **Q14** - **Can a tutorial pause and resume?**
- (a) Save the current tutorial and step in the plugin's data. After a reload, offer "Resume your tutorial?".
- (b) Keep it only while Obsidian is open; a restart ends it.

➡️ Go with (b) for the prototype and (a) when it ships. Saving and resuming means handling steps whose UI state is gone after a restart, which tells us nothing about whether AI-generated tours work at all.

Settled: **Q17 = (b)**, a dedicated `/api/obsidian/tutorial` endpoint.

One correction to my earlier summary: the welcome notice doesn't stop the tour right after starting it. That `stop()` call is in `onunload`, which is correct. So that's not a bug.

## What eng-1505 built

There's one work-in-progress commit (`c1f4e258`, Mar 31) with **the same 3-step tour built twice**:

1. Click the telescope ribbon icon to open Discourse Context.
2. Press Cmd+P. This step has no element to highlight, so it's a floating card, and it moves on when the palette (`.prompt`) appears.
3. The palette is highlighted with "type Create discourse node", and Finish ends the tour.

The welcome notice ("Welcome to Discourse Graphs! Take a quick tour") starts the **driver.js** version. The "Start onboarding tour" command starts the **custom React** version. There's a commented-out line where you switched between the two.

## How they compare

| | Custom React | driver.js |
|---|---|---|
| **How steps are defined** | A list of plain data objects (`OnboardingStep[]`). The tour logic is a single hook that works through any list. | Three phases written as code (`startPhase1/2/3`). Each new step means writing a new method. |
| **Moving to the next step** | Built into the step data: `advanceOn: {event}` for a click, `{waitForSelector}` for waiting until an element appears, or `manualAdvance`. | driver.js only moves on when its own Next button is clicked. Advancing on the user's actual click or on the palette opening is extra code outside driver.js, which is why the tour is split into separate phases. |
| **Spotlight** | A transparent box over the target with a huge shadow that dims everything else. `pointer-events: none` lets clicks reach the real UI everywhere. | driver.js's own dimmed layer, which by default blocks clicks outside the highlighted element. |
| **Steps with no element** | Built-in centered card. | A hand-built floating card outside driver.js. |
| **Styling** | Inline styles with hardcoded z-index values (10001–10003), using 17 theme variables. | A 307-line stylesheet that restyles every driver.js part with 22 Obsidian theme variables. **This is the more polished look.** |
| **Cleanup and Escape** | Escape listener is added in the normal (bubbling) phase. Every frame it re-measures the target's position. | Collects every listener into one cleanup list, with Escape caught early (capture phase). **This is the tidier lifecycle handling.** |
| **Missing target** | Shows an "Element not found" card. | Nothing handles it; driver.js just highlights nothing. |

## Where your accuracy work is

The fine-tuning you did is mostly in the parts **both versions share**:

- the exact element handles: the telescope's `aria-label` and `.prompt` for the palette
- the step order
- the idea that a step with nothing to point at becomes a floating card
- detecting the palette opening as "done"

All of that carries over whichever engine we choose. The driver.js version adds better styling and cleanup, and both can be ported.

The deciding factor is the AI. A generated tutorial is **data**: a list of any length that we've never seen before. The custom version already runs data. With the driver.js version, the steps are code, so we'd have to write a general step runner around driver.js anyway. At that point driver.js would only draw the spotlight and popup, and every hard part, like waiting for elements and advancing on user actions, would be ours.

❓ **Q18** - **Which version to use?**
- (a) The custom React version, plus the driver.js version's stylesheet (renamed to our own class names), its cleanup list, and its early Escape handling. Keep all your handles and step sequence.
- (b) Our own step runner that uses driver.js only to draw the spotlight and popup.
- (c) Keep the driver.js phases as they are.

➡️ Go with (a). It runs steps from data, lets clicks reach the real UI (which the "create a node" modal needs), and handles missing targets. The driver.js version's best parts, the stylesheet and the cleanup, move across easily.

Pick (b) if you liked driver.js's animation and positioning. It's MIT-licensed and small, so either is fine to ship.

One Escape detail matters for (a): inside an Obsidian modal, a page-level listener can't stop Escape. Obsidian handles it first through its own key scope. So the tour needs to register its own key scope, not just listen on `document`.

Once you've answered Q18 and confirmed the shared understanding from my last message, I'll write the implementation plan.

# Obsidian AI tutorial: prototype plan

Experimental branch `obsidian-ai-tutorial`. There is no Linear ticket yet.

A user describes what they want to do. The website asks the model to build a tutorial from
building blocks, using the docs as context. The plugin then plays the tutorial as a
spotlight tour, and each step moves on when the user actually does it.

ship_when_verified: no (this is a prototype; we decide whether to ship after the self-check
and the user sessions)

## Decisions (from the grilling session)

| # | Decision |
|---|---|
| Q1 | Users: people new to both Obsidian and Discourse Graphs, plus Obsidian users new to Discourse Graphs |
| Q2 | Scope: Discourse Graphs plus the core Obsidian basics it relies on |
| Q3 | Prototype first, then ship to real users behind an experimental setting |
| Q4/Q9 | Three kinds of step: tested blocks → general blocks checked against the live app (command, ribbon icon, settings tab) → text-only steps |
| Q5 | A command first, then a welcome screen on first launch (M6) |
| Q6 | A "New to Obsidian?" question before generating, plus a "Skip, I know this" button on each basics step |
| Q7/Q17 | A dedicated `/api/obsidian/tutorial` endpoint; the website adds the docs and examples to the prompt |
| Q10/Q15 | All the Obsidian docs (about 29k tokens, cached) go with every request, read from the website itself so they're always current |
| Q11 | The model receives: the user's prompt, node and relation type names, the live command list, and the plugin version. Never note titles or note contents |
| Q12 | Tutorials create real notes. The end screen lists them and offers to delete them |
| Q13 | A failed step falls back to a text card with Skip and Mark done. "I'm stuck → rewrite" is deferred |
| Q14 | No pause and resume in the prototype |
| Q16 | The 4 use-case pages become hand-written ideal tutorials, used both as worked examples and as the self-check's comparison set |
| Q18 | Port eng-1505's custom React version and add the driver.js version's stylesheet, cleanup list and early Escape handling |
| Q8 | Measure with a self-check of about 20 prompts plus 3–5 people trying it. Analytics come later |

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  U[User prompt + New to Obsidian?] --> M[GenerateTutorialModal]
  M --> C[Vault context: node/relation types, command list, version]
  C --> API["/api/obsidian/tutorial"]
  D[content/obsidian docs] --> API
  G[Ideal tutorials] --> API
  API -->|structured steps| V[Check steps locally]
  V --> E[Tour engine]
  B[Block library] --> E
  E --> O[Spotlight overlay]
  E --> S[End screen: notes created]
```

## Step format (shared by the plugin and the website)

```ts
type TutorialStep = { title: string; body: string; basics?: boolean } & (
  | { kind: "block"; block: BlockId; params: Record<string, string> }
  | { kind: "command"; commandId: string }        // must be in the live command list
  | { kind: "ribbon"; label: string }              // must match a ribbon icon's label
  | { kind: "settings-tab"; tabId: string }
  | { kind: "text" }
);
```

Each block in the plugin defines:
- `id`
- `params`
- `target(params)`: the element to spotlight, or `null` to show a centered card
- `placement`
- `watchDone(plugin, params, done)`: returns a cleanup function

Done-checks use **plugin state** wherever possible, with DOM checks as the fallback:
- **Node created:** listen to `metadataCache` "changed" for a new file whose `nodeTypeId` matches.
- **Relation added:** listen for changes to `relations.json`, following the pattern in
  `relationsIndex.ts`.

**Checking steps locally:** if a step names a block, command or ribbon label the app doesn't
have, it becomes `text`, so a bad step never breaks the tour.

## Milestones (in build order)

Each milestone ends with its own verification. Unit tests are committed in `src/**/__tests__/`.
CDP scenarios stay in the scratchpad.

### M1. Tour engine port (a fixed tour, no AI)
- Bring eng-1505's approach A into `apps/obsidian/src/components/tutorial/`:
  - the step data, the tour hook, the overlay, and the overlay manager
  - the stylesheet, rewritten for our own class names in `src/styles/tutorial.css`, using
    theme variables
- Fixes made during the port:
  - Replace every-frame position polling with `ResizeObserver`, plus updates on scroll and
    layout changes.
  - Collect all listeners in one cleanup list and stop the tour on plugin unload.
  - Handle Escape with an Obsidian keymap `Scope`, not a `document` listener, because a
    modal handles Escape first.
  - Make sure the spotlight never blocks clicks on Obsidian modals.
  - Keep the "element not found" card, and turn it into the Q13 fallback (Skip / Mark done).
- Replay eng-1505's 3-step tour through the new format, behind a dev-only command.
- **Verify:**
  - Vitest for step order and for skipping basics steps.
  - Use `dg-obsidian-cdp-verify` to play the 3-step tour in testVault, with screenshots of
    each step, plus Escape inside the create-node modal.

### M2. Block library and the 4 ideal tutorials
- Blocks, starting with these:
  - `open-command-palette`, `create-node(type)`, `open-discourse-context`,
    `add-relation(type)`, `link-notes`, `open-canvas`, `open-settings`
  - basics blocks: `create-note`, `open-file-explorer`
- General blocks:
  - `command`: needs typed `app.commands` access, added in `src/types/obsidian-unofficial.d.ts`
  - `ribbon`
  - `settings-tab`
- Write the 4 use-case pages as ideal tutorials made of steps, in
  `apps/website/app/api/obsidian/tutorial/examples/` (stored on the website, which needs them
  for the prompt).
- **Spike first (a few hours):** find out how to detect that a command ran (Obsidian has no
  event for it) and that a settings tab opened (Settings is a separate window in Obsidian
  1.13). If neither can be detected reliably, those steps fall back to a Done button.
- **Verify:**
  - Vitest for the local step-checking and downgrading.
  - CDP plays each of the 4 ideal tutorials end to end in testVault: every spotlight lands
    on its element, and every done-check fires on the real action.

### M3. Website endpoint
- Add `apps/website/app/api/obsidian/tutorial/route.ts`, following the pattern of
  `app/api/ai/extract/route.ts`: `anthropicConfig.formatRequestBody` + `fetch`, with
  `runtime = "nodejs"`.
  - Reuse `cors` and `handleOptionsRequest`.
  - Structured output uses `outputSchema`, which becomes `output_config.format`.
- Docs: read `content/obsidian/**` at request time and cache it in memory. On Vercel, add
  `outputFileTracingIncludes` so the files are deployed with the function. This has never
  been done here, so check it on a preview deploy. Fallback: generate the docs into a module
  at build time and import it.
- Prompt: system instructions, the docs, the examples, the block list with its parameters,
  the user's vault context, and the user's prompt.
  - Choose the model with the `claude-api` skill. `DEFAULT_MODEL_ID` is the starting point.
  - Check the reply against the step format on the server too.
- **Verify:**
  - Vitest for request checking and the reply format (with the model mocked).
  - Run the local website and `curl` it with 3 real prompts, checking the replies are valid
    step lists.

### M4. Plugin end to end
- A "Generate a tutorial" command, behind `FEATURE_FLAGS` (the admin panel), opens a
  `GenerateTutorialModal`. The modal has the prompt, the "New to Obsidian?" question, and a
  loading and error state.
- Gather the vault context and call the endpoint with `requestUrl` at `nextApiRoot()`. Check
  the steps locally, then run the tour.
- The end screen lists the notes created during the tutorial and offers to delete them (it
  needs a confirmation step).
- **Verify:** use CDP against the local website with 3 prompts:
  - one from someone new to Obsidian
  - one from someone who knows Obsidian
  - one that's off-topic, such as "make a recipe database", which should mostly produce
    text steps

  Screenshots go into the scratchpad.

### M5. Self-check and user sessions
- A script runs about 20 test prompts (kept separate from the 4 examples) against the
  endpoint, then measures:
  - the share of steps that are tested blocks, general blocks or text
  - how many steps were downgraded
  - whether each tutorial can be completed: CDP replays every tutorial that has no text steps
- Run 3–5 people through it (you run these sessions) and note where they get stuck.
- **Output:** a short findings page used to decide whether to ship.

### M6. Welcome screen on first launch (only if M5 looks good)
- On the first `onLayoutReady` after install, show a welcome screen with the prompt field.
  Remember that it was shown in settings.
- **Verify:** CDP with a fresh vault shows it once and not after a reload.

## Out of scope for the prototype
- Pause and resume, "I'm stuck → rewrite", analytics, rate limiting, mobile layout.
- Sending note contents to the model.
- Tutorials for other plugins.

## Blockers for shipping
- Rate limiting on the endpoint, since the existing LLM endpoints have no login check.
- Saving and resuming progress.
- Docs written for a newer version than the user has installed: we send the plugin version
  now, but nothing uses it yet.

## Risks
- **Detecting command and settings-tab steps (M2 spike).** If it isn't reliable, the
  general-block tier becomes a spotlight with a Done button.
- **Screenshot-heavy docs.** The text alone gives the model less to go on for UI flows, which
  is the reason for the block library.
- **Tutorial notes in testVault.** Testing creates real notes in testVault, which also holds

The plan is written to [.claude/plan.md](.claude/plan.md). It's gitignored, so it won't end up in a commit.

It builds in six stages, and each one ends with its own verification step:

1. **Port the tour engine.** Bring over the custom React version from eng-1505, with the driver.js version's stylesheet, cleanup list and early Escape handling. While porting, fix the known gaps:
   - replace the every-frame position checks
   - use Obsidian's key handling for Escape, so it works inside modals
   - make sure the spotlight never blocks clicks on Obsidian's modals

   Your 3-step tour then replays through the new format, checked in testVault over CDP.
2. **Block library and the 4 ideal tutorials** written from the use-case pages. Each ideal tutorial is played end to end in real Obsidian.
3. **Website endpoint** `/api/obsidian/tutorial`. The website reads the docs from `content/obsidian/` and asks the model for a structured list of steps.
4. **Plugin end to end:** a command behind the admin-panel feature flag, the prompt window, local checking of the generated steps, the tour itself, and the end screen offering to delete the notes it created.
5. **Self-check and user sessions:** about 20 test prompts scored automatically, plus 3–5 people trying it. The result decides whether to ship.
6. **Welcome screen on first launch**, only if stage 5 looks good.

There are two unknowns in the plan, each with a fallback:

- **Docs on Vercel:** nothing here has read the docs folder from an API route before, so it may not be deployed with the function. Stage 3 checks this on a preview deploy. If it fails, the docs get built into the website when it's deployed. That still has no copy for you to maintain, which keeps your intent from Q10.
- **Detecting command and settings-tab steps:** Obsidian has no event for "a command ran", and Settings is a separate window in Obsidian 1.13. Stage 2 starts with a few hours' investigation. If neither can be detected reliably, those steps get a spotlight plus a Done button instead.

If you approve the plan, I'll record it as the approved plan in your session context with `/checkpoint`, then start stage 1.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/trang.doan/.claude/skills/checkpoint

# Checkpoint — record session context

Persist the **reasoning layer** of this work session (goal, decisions, dead ends,
constraints, next step) to the Obsidian vault, keyed to the current worktree.
Files are plain markdown written directly — no MCP, no Obsidian required running.

## Steps

### 1. Resolve where to write
Run the helper from the current worktree:

```bash
bash ~/.claude/scripts/session-context.sh resolve
```

It prints `TICKET`, `BRANCH`, `WORKTREE`, `SESSION_DIR`, `CONTEXT_FILE`,
`LOG_FILE`, `STAMP`, `CONTEXT_EXISTS` and creates the folders. **Only write to the
`CONTEXT_FILE` and `LOG_FILE` paths it gives you** — never elsewhere in the vault.
If it errors (not a git repo / detached HEAD), tell the user and stop.

### 2. Read existing context if present
If `CONTEXT_EXISTS=yes`, read `CONTEXT_FILE` first so you UPDATE it rather than
overwrite history. Digest sections get rewritten; accreting sections get appended.

### 3. Gather the reasoning layer
Reconstruct from this session's conversation + git. If a ticket id is present and
Linear is available, you may fetch the title/URL with `mcp__linear-server__get_issue`.
Apply the **extraction rubric** below to decide what is worth recording.

### 4. Write `_context.md`
Use the template at `~/.claude/skills/checkpoint/template.md` as the structure.
- If new file: fill the template. Set `created`/`updated` to today, `sessions: 1`.
- If updating: rewrite digest sections (TL;DR, Approved plan, Current state, Next
  step, Open questions, key_files, status), **append** to accreting sections (Key
  decisions, Dead ends, Constraints, Gotchas, Interventions) with a dated bullet,
  bump `updated` to today and increment `sessions`.
- **Approved plan:** write it only when the user approves a plan (gate 1), verbatim
  as approved: Mermaid diagram, per-file/module intent bullets, and the exact line
  `ship_when_verified: yes|no` (`no` unless the user said ship when verified).
  /create-pr parses this heading and line; don't rename or reformat them.
- **Interventions:** append `- [YYYY-MM-DD] <what the human had to do> — <why the agent couldn't>`
  whenever the user had to step in.

### 5. Append a log snapshot
Write a short dated entry to `LOG_FILE` (a fresh file — no append needed):
a 3–6 line summary of what THIS session accomplished + what changed since last time.
This is the immutable audit trail; `_context.md` is the living digest.

### 6. Confirm
Tell the user what you wrote (context file + log file paths) and the one-line Next step.

## Extraction rubric — what to record (keep it concise)

**The test:** record a line only if it would otherwise have to be *re-derived* or
would prevent *repeating a mistake*. Ask: *"What do I know now that I didn't at
session start, that isn't already in Linear, git, or the code?"*

**DO record (the reasoning layer — it evaporates when the session ends):**
- Scope agreement: how the ticket was interpreted, what's in/out of scope.
- Decisions: what + why + what was rejected + what would make us revisit it.
- Dead ends: what was tried that failed, and why.
- Constraints/preferences the user stated ("ship by Fri", "don't touch billing").
- Gotchas: environmental facts learned the hard way.
- Next step + open questions + current status.

**Do NOT record (noise / lives elsewhere):**
- Activity logs ("edited foo.ts, ran tests") — record outcomes, not keystrokes.
- Anything copy-pasteable from the diff, git history, or the Linear ticket body.
- Resolved questions — delete them or fold the answer into a decision.
- Restating how the code works — that's what the code is for.

**Mark uncertainty** explicitly (`*assumed*`, `*unchecked*`). Prefer 8 sharp lines
over 40 vague ones — this must stay skimmable for the user, not just parseable by an agent.

You are working on the Obsidian plugin that implements the Discourse Graph protocol.

## Dependencies

Prefer existing dependencies from package.json.

## Obsidian Style Guide

Use the obsidian style guide from help.obsidian.md/style-guide and docs.obsidian.md/Developer+policies.

### Icons

Platform-native UI.
Lucide and custom Obsidian icons can be used alongside detailed elements to provide a visual representation of a feature.

Example: In the ribbon on the left, select Create new canvas ( lucide-layout-dashboard.svg > icon ) to create a canvas in the same folder as the active file.

Guidelines for icons

Store icons in the Attachments/icons folder.
Add the prefix lucide- before the Lucide icon name.
Add the prefix obsidian-icon- before the Obsidian icon name.
Example: The icon for creating a new canvas should be named lucide-layout-dashboard.

Use the SVG version of the icons available.
Icons should be 18 pixels in width, 18 pixels in height, and have a stroke width of 1.5. You can adjust these settings in the SVG data.
Adjusting size and stroke in an SVG.
Utilize the icon anchor in embedded images, to tweak the spacing around the icon so that it aligns neatly with the text in the vicinity.
Icons should be surrounded by parenthesis. ( lucide-cog.svg > icon )
Example: ( ![[lucide-cog.svg#icon]] )

### Function guides

- Any function that deals with querying vault's frontmatter, default to using Datacore API first, then write fallback where you use `plugin.app.vault.getMarkdownFiles()` to iterate through each file's frontmatter

## Plugin Store Guidelines

These rules must be followed for the plugin to be accepted into the Obsidian community plugin store.

### Security

- Never use `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, or `insertAdjacentHTML` with user-controlled content
- Use Obsidian DOM helpers instead: `createEl()`, `createDiv()`, `createSpan()`

### App instance

- Always use `this.app` — never the global `app` object

### Event listeners

- Register all event listeners via `this.registerEvent()` so they are automatically cleaned up on plugin unload

### UI text

- Use sentence case in settings headings and labels (not title case)
- Prefer `setHeading()` over raw HTML heading elements (`<h1>`, `<h2>`, etc.)

### Commands

- Do not set default hotkeys — they conflict with other plugins
- Use the correct callback type: `callback` for always-available commands, `checkCallback` when the command is conditionally available, or the editor variants for editor-scoped commands
- Do not manually prepend the plugin ID to command IDs — Obsidian adds it automatically

### Workspace

- Do not store references to custom views — look them up fresh each time they are needed
  Don't do this:
  `this.registerView(MY_VIEW_TYPE, () => this.view = new MyCustomView());`
  Do this instead:
  `this.registerView(MY_VIEW_TYPE, () => new MyCustomView());`
  To access the view from your plugin, use `Workspace.getActiveLeavesOfType():`

```
for (let leaf of app.workspace.getActiveLeavesOfType(MY_VIEW_TYPE)) {
  let view = leaf.view;
  if (view instanceof MyCustomView) {
    // ...
  }
}
```

- Do not detach leaves during plugin unload

### Editor

- Prefer the Editor API over `Vault.modify()` when the note is currently open in the editor
- Prefer `Vault.process()` instead of `Vault.modify()` to modify a file in the background

### Mobile compatibility

- Node.js and Electron APIs (`fs`, `crypto`, `os`) are unavailable on mobile
- If the plugin targets mobile, use web API equivalents: `SubtleCrypto` instead of `crypto`, `navigator.clipboard` for clipboard access
- Regex lookbehind assertions are not supported on some mobile — avoid them if possible

### Code quality

- Use `const`/`let` — never `var`
- Prefer `async`/`await` over `.then()` chains
- Minimize `console.log` — remove debug logs before shipping
- Do not hardcode styles inline — use CSS classes and Obsidian's CSS variables

## Unit tests

Vitest runs the plugin's pure logic in a Node environment: `pnpm test:unit` (or `pnpm test:watch` while working). The repository-wide `pnpm ci:validate` picks it up through the `test:unit` script.

- Put tests in `src/**/__tests__/<module>.test.ts`, next to the code they cover. Tests covering the test scaffolding itself live in `test/`; those two globs are the whole of `include` in `vitest.config.mts`.
- Import the module under test through the `~` alias, as the source does.
- `obsidian` ships type declarations with no runtime entry point, so `vitest.config.mts` aliases it to `test/obsidianStub.ts`. Add to that stub whatever a new test needs to load its module; use `vi.mock("obsidian")` in the test itself when the test needs to assert on a call.
- Obsidian's own objects are large. Build the slice the code path reads and cast it (`{ metadataCache: … } as unknown as App`) rather than constructing a whole `App` or `TFile`.
- Logic that needs a live vault, editor, or workspace is not covered here — extract the decision into a util and test that.

### Keeping the stub honest

The stub is hand-written, so it can be wrong about the API today and can fall behind when the `obsidian` dependency is bumped. Two mechanisms catch that. Each runs under exactly one command, so run `pnpm ci:validate` to get both.

`test/obsidianStub.conformance.ts` type-checks each stub member against the real declaration. It is type-only and matches none of the vitest globs, so only `pnpm check-types` enforces it. Keep it inside the `tsconfig.json` include, or the drift check disappears with no signal.

- Members with real behavior are fully conformant.
- Shells, which exist only so an importing module loads, are checked for the export name alone. When a shell gains behavior, move it to the conformant group.
- Every export must appear in one group or the other, so adding one without classifying it fails the build.

`test/obsidianStub.test.ts` pins the behavior the stub reimplements, which the type checker cannot see. It is type-checked like any other file, but only `pnpm test:unit` runs its assertions.

### Verifying the stub

Type declarations cannot tell you what a function returns for a given input, so do not guess it. Obsidian ships its implementation in `obsidian.asar`, in the resources directory of the installed app, and the current cases were settled by reading it. Two details it settled: `normalizePath("/")` returns `"/"`, and `TFolder.isRoot()` tests `path === "/"` rather than a null parent.

The bundle is minified, so it takes two steps: find the exported name to learn its minified name, then find that function. The example below is a macOS path; on Windows and Linux locate `obsidian.asar` under the install directory and substitute it.

```
node -e 'const s=require("fs").readFileSync("/Applications/Obsidian.app/Contents/Resources/obsidian.asar","utf8");
  const i=s.indexOf("normalizePath:()=>");
  console.log(s.slice(i, i+80));'
```

Read the behavior and reimplement it; do not paste the bundle's code into this repository. Pin whatever you learn in `obsidianStub.test.ts`, and name the test `diverges: …` when the stub deliberately does something else.

# Obsidian CDP verify

## The one command

From the worktree root:

```sh
node ~/.claude/skills/dg-obsidian-cdp-verify/scripts/run.mjs \
  --marker "<string only this change's bundle contains>" \
  --scenario path/to/scenarios.mjs [--scenario more.mjs] [--port 9222] [--skip-build]
```

It runs claim → doctor → launch → deliver → scenarios → cleanup and prints the `last-run.json` path, the scenario matrix, and the `pr-evidence` args. Exit codes: 0 all pass, 1 failure, 2 no vault available or vault locked, 3 marker missing.

On exit 2 with `candidates`, follow the `obsidian-vault` skill: ask Trang which vault to take, then run `vault.mjs claim --take` and rerun.

Write scenario files in the session scratchpad, not the repo.

## Launch

- With no `--slot`, the vault is this worktree's `obsidian-vault` lease. `run.mjs` claims a free one if the worktree has no lease yet. This keeps the CDP run in the vault the worktree's watcher builds into.
- `--slot N` is a legacy override. It's a 1-based index into `OBSIDIAN_VERIFY_VAULTS` in `<worktree>/apps/obsidian/.env` and bypasses leases, so use it only when Trang names a slot.
- If Obsidian is running on the debug port, the script attaches.
- If it's running without the port, the script quits Obsidian and relaunches it with `--remote-debugging-port`. Trang approved this; the windows come back.
- If it isn't running, the script launches it with the port.
- It then opens the slot vault through `obsidian://open?path=` and waits for a page target where `.workspace` exists and `app.vault.adapter.basePath` matches the vault.
- It writes the lock `<vault>/.obsidian/dg-verify.lock` (`{pid, branch, startedAt}`) and releases it in `finally`.

## Doctor

`scripts/doctor.mjs [--slot N]` is read-only and prints JSON: the resolved vault, the lock and the Obsidian state. It exits 2 if the worktree has no lease, or if another live run holds the lock. A lock left by a dead pid is ignored.

## Deliver

`scripts/deliver.mjs --marker <str>` also runs on its own.

1. `OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_PATH=<slot plugin dir> tsx scripts/build.ts` runs once in `apps/obsidian`. It also writes `apps/obsidian/dist`, which is gitignored.
2. It greps the vault's `main.js` for `--marker` and fails if the marker is absent.
3. It reloads the plugin. The plugin id and folder are resolved from the manifests.
4. It greps again.
5. It warns about other worktrees' apps/obsidian `dev.ts` watchers that mirror into this vault. Your own worktree's watcher builds the same code, so it isn't flagged.

The harness also hashes `main.js` before and after the scenarios. If it changed, the run is marked invalid.

## Drive: scenario contract

A module's `export default` is one scenario or an array of them:

```js
export default {
  name: "Search modal renders",                 // matrix row + screenshot name
  input: "run open-node-search",                // matrix text
  expected: "modal with a textbox and footer",  // matrix text
  setup: async (ctx) => ({ /* state; snapshot anything you change */ }),  // optional
  run: async ({ client, json, vault }, state) => {
    await client.evaluate(`return app.commands.executeCommandById(${json(`${vault.pluginId}:open-node-search`)});`);
    await client.waitFor(`!!document.querySelector(".dg-node-search-modal [role=textbox]")`);
    return client.evaluate(`document.querySelectorAll(".dg-search-footer-action").length`);
  },
  expect: (actual, state) => ({ pass: actual > 0, actual: `${actual} footer actions` }),  // or a boolean
  teardown: async (ctx, state) => {},           // optional: restore what setup changed
};
```

- `ctx` has `client`, `vault` (`root`, `pluginId`, `pluginDir`), `branch`, `json`, `verifyPath(name)` and `writeNote(name, body)`. `writeNote` creates or overwrites `_verify/<branch>/<name>` and returns its path.
- `client` has `evaluate`, `waitFor`, `key`, `typeText`, `pressEscape`, `screenshot`, `reloadPlugin`, `clearModals` and `send` (raw CDP).
- The harness does these for you:
  - Before each scenario, it clears modals and restores the layout captured at the start of the run.
  - After `run`, it takes a screenshot.
  - A thrown error becomes a failing row.
- The worked example is `examples/insert-link-at-cursor.mjs` (ENG-2114, 3 scenarios).

## Evidence

- The artifacts go to `<worktree>/local/obsidian-cdp/artifacts/<branch>/<runStamp>/`: `<n>-<slug>.png` and `last-run.json` (`results[]` of `{scenario, input, expected, actual, pass, screenshot}`).
- Paste the printed matrix into create-pr's Evidence section.
- Upload the screenshots with pr-evidence, using the printed args:

```sh
./apps/roam/node_modules/.bin/tsx ~/.claude/skills/pr-evidence/upload.ts --harness obsidian-cdp <printed args>
```

## Cleanup

- Cleanup dismisses modals (Escape, then force-removes leftover `.modal-container`), restores the baseline layout and releases the lock.
- **It never deletes folders or notes.** `_verify/<branch>/` persists, and reruns overwrite its notes.
- Scenarios that change vault or app settings must restore them in `teardown`.

## Gotchas

These are the ones the code can't handle for you.

| Symptom | Cause / fix |
| --- | --- |
| Double-handled keypress | Pass `type` to `client.key` only through its loop. Never send your own `keyDown`. |
| `editor.hasFocus()` false while focus looks right | This can't be measured over CDP. Assert the consequence instead, e.g. the cursor moved past the inserted text. |
| File content assertion fails, editor looks right | Saves are debounced (about 2s). `waitFor` on `app.vault.read(...)`, and don't read once. |
| `getLeaf(true)` throws "No tab group found" | Every markdown leaf was detached. Use `getLeaf("tab")`. |
| Top-level `await` throws in `evaluate` | Bodies run in a plain function. Return an async IIFE or a promise chain. |
| `iterateRootLeaves` count caps at 2 | A truthy callback return stops the iteration. Use a block body `{ n++; }`. |
| Escape handler in a modal child never wins | Obsidian's modal scope runs first. Push a `Scope` with `app.keymap.pushScope`. |
| Styling CodeMirror spans disappears on focus or scroll | Use a CM6 decoration, not MutationObserver stamping. A widget's `ignoreEvent()` must stay `true` for clicks. |
| Selectors from an old ENG example don't match | The UI drifts. The node search input is now a contenteditable `[role=textbox]`, not an `<input>`. |
| Flaky failure that looks like a code bug | Trang may be using the app mid-run. Rerun before believing a single observation. |
| Timers stall, writes land minutes late | Focus emulation normally prevents this. If it recurs, check `document.visibilityState` and ask Trang to show the window. |
| zsh eats `${VAR}` in `node -e` | Write scenarios to `.mjs` files. |
| `waitFor` on an IIFE always times out | `evaluate` adds an outer `return` only when the code contains no `return`. An IIFE with an inner `return` evaluates to `undefined`, so write `return (() => { ... })()`. |
| A note written in `setup` is randomly missing from search results | Datacore indexes new files after the metadata cache, and the search loads through Datacore. After `writeNote`, also `waitFor` `dc.query("@page and exists(nodeTypeId)")` to include the path. |

---
name: reference-obsidian-watcher-ignores-css
description: apps/obsidian dev watcher only rebuilds styles.css when a TS file's content changes; CSS-only edits never reach the vault
metadata:
  type: reference
---

The apps/obsidian dev watcher (`scripts/dev.ts` → esbuild watch) combines `src/styles/*.css` into `styles.css` inside an esbuild `onEnd` hook. esbuild only watches the files the bundle imports, so editing only a `.css` file never triggers a rebuild. `touch` doesn't work either, because esbuild skips rebuilds when the content is unchanged.

**How to apply:** after a CSS-only edit, run `NODE_ENV=development npx tsx scripts/build.ts` in apps/obsidian (it mirrors to `OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_PATH` and keeps dev-only code). Then grep the vault's `styles.css` for the new rule before trusting a CDP run. Plain `build.ts` without `NODE_ENV` makes a production build, which drops `process.env.NODE_ENV !== "production"` code. Related: [[reference_obsidian_contested_vault_plugin_dir]], [[reference_cdp_verify_harness_contract]].

content.text:
M1 is done: your 3-step sample tour from eng-1505 now runs through the new engine in real Obsidian. All 7 CDP scenarios and 9 unit tests pass, and types and lint are clean. Nothing is committed yet.

**What the CDP runs in testVault showed:**
- **Step 1:** the telescope icon gets an accent ring and the card sits to its right. A real mouse click on the icon moves the tour on and opens discourse context.
- **Step 2:** a floating card at the bottom right. Cmd+P still opens the palette while the tour is running, and the tour moves on when it opens.
- **Step 3:** the ring goes around the palette, with a Finish button.
- **Escape while the palette is open** closes the palette but keeps the tour. With nothing open, Escape ends the tour and puts Obsidian's keyboard handling back as it was.
- **Target missing** (for example, the ribbon is hidden): after about 600ms the card says the element isn't on screen and offers Skip and Mark done, which work.
- **Plugin reload during a tour** leaves nothing behind on the page.

**Changes from eng-1505:**
- Clicking outside the spotlight no longer ends the tour, so users can click into Obsidian's windows during a step.
- Steps complete through page-level listeners, so they still work if Obsidian redraws the element.
- Position is still checked every frame, but the overlay only redraws when the target moves.
- Styles are in a CSS file using Obsidian's theme colours.
- A target that disappears mid-step gets the fallback card instead of leaving a blank screen.

**What I got wrong along the way:**
- I told you a very large box-shadow doesn't paint in Chromium, and briefly replaced it with an SVG backdrop. A high-contrast red test showed the shadow does paint. On a dark theme, 50% black is just very subtle in screenshots. I reverted the change and kept only the accent-coloured ring, because that's what actually makes the target stand out.
- Some test runs used stale CSS, because the dev watcher doesn't rebuild after CSS-only edits. I saved that as a memory.

The code is in `apps/obsidian/src/components/tutorial/`, plus `src/styles/tutorial.css` and the dev-only command at the end of [registerCommands.ts](apps/obsidian/src/utils/registerCommands.ts). The checkpoint's current state and next step are updated, and the scenario script is in the scratchpad.

A suggested addition to CLAUDE.md, since it's a general lesson: *"Before concluding a visual element doesn't render, re-test it with a high-contrast colour; dark themes hide low-contrast changes in screenshots."*

Should I commit M1 and add that line to CLAUDE.md? M2 starts with the investigation into detecting when a command ran or a settings tab opened.

content.text:
Here's where the AI tutorial experiment stands. In short: the plan is agreed and stage 1 of 6 (M1) is built and verified, but none of it is committed yet.

## What's been done

**1. Setup**
- Created the worktree `.claude/worktrees/obsidian-ai-tutorial` on branch `obsidian-ai-tutorial`. There's no Linear ticket.
- Took over **testVault** for this worktree, with your OK.
- Found the earlier prototype on `origin/eng-1505-timebox-to-create-skeleton-for-onboarding-user-flow`. It was never opened as a PR.

**2. Design**
- We settled 18 decisions through grilling. The main ones:
  - **Blocks:** the AI picks and orders tested building blocks; it never invents which on-screen element to point at.
  - **Endpoint:** a dedicated website endpoint, `/api/obsidian/tutorial`, which adds the docs to the prompt.
  - **Engine:** the custom React version from eng-1505, not driver.js.
- You approved a 6-stage plan: tour engine → block library → website endpoint → end-to-end plugin flow → self-check and user sessions → welcome screen on first launch.
- The plan and decisions are saved in `testVault/AI_sessions/obsidian-ai-tutorial/_context.md`.

**3. M1, the tour engine, is built but not committed**
- New code is in `apps/obsidian/src/components/tutorial/` and `src/styles/tutorial.css`.
- A dev-only command, "Play sample tutorial (dev)", replays your 3-step tour from eng-1505.
- **Changes from eng-1505:**
  - clicks still reach Obsidian's own windows during a step
  - Escape closes the palette or a modal first, and only ends the tour when nothing else is open
  - steps still complete if Obsidian redraws the element
  - a missing target shows a fallback card with Skip and Mark done
  - the tour cleans itself up when the plugin unloads
  - the target gets an accent-coloured ring
- **Verified:**
  - 9 unit tests pass.
  - 7 scenarios pass in real Obsidian, with screenshots.

**4. Lessons recorded**
- Saved as a memory: the Obsidian dev watcher doesn't rebuild after CSS-only changes.
- Also recorded: a false lead where I wrongly blamed Chromium for not drawing the spotlight. It was drawn; dimming is just hard to see on a dark theme.

## Current state, 11 days on
- M1 is still **uncommitted**: one modified file and two new ones.
- The branch is still at the old `origin/main` it started from. Main has moved on since, for example ENG-2361.
- The Obsidian dev watcher is **no longer running**. It stopped when the last session ended.
- Still waiting on you: whether to commit M1, and whether to add the visual-check lesson to CLAUDE.md.

## Next step
1. **Commit M1** and bring the branch up to date with main.
2. **Start M2 with a short investigation:** can we reliably tell when the user ran a particular command or opened a particular settings tab? Obsidian has no event for either, and Settings is a separate window in Obsidian 1.13. The answer decides whether those steps complete automatically or need a Done button.
3. **Then build the block library** (create a node, add a relation, open discourse context, and so on) and turn the 4 use-case doc pages into ideal step-by-step tutorials. Each one gets played end to end in Obsidian.

Shall I commit M1 and restart the watcher on testVault so M2 can begin?
yes, commit M1 and start M2

---
name: reference_obsidian_settings_separate_window
description: Obsidian 1.13 opens Settings in its own window; CDP mouse input to the main target can't reach it
metadata:
  type: reference
---
In Obsidian 1.13 (seen on 1.13.7, dgDevVault), `app.setting.open()` renders settings in a separate window ("Settings - <vault> - Obsidian"). `app.setting.activeTab.containerEl` is connected, but not to the main `document`, so `document.querySelector` finds nothing and CDP `Input.dispatchMouseEvent` on the main page target never reaches it.

For a Settings check in a dg-obsidian-cdp-verify scenario, query from `app.setting.activeTab.containerEl` and drive it with DOM events. For inputs, use that window's native value setter plus `input`, then `focusout`. Say so in the scenario's input column. Related: [[reference_obsidian_cdp_driving]].

Also: the "Relation types" tab button in `Settings.tsx` has no `discourse-tab` class (the other tabs do), so select tabs by text.

To screenshot Settings (CDP `Page.captureScreenshot` only sees the main window): in an `evaluate`, find the window with `require("electron").remote.BrowserWindow.getAllWindows().find(w => w.getTitle().startsWith("Settings"))`, call `await win.webContents.capturePage()` with no rect, and write `img.toPNG()` with `require("fs")`. Then crop with ffmpeg using the row's `getBoundingClientRect()` × `devicePixelRatio`. Passing a rect to `capturePage` cropped the wrong area (seen on ENG-2363).

The spike is done. Here's what it found:

**1. "The user ran command X" can be detected reliably.** ✅
- Wrapping the command's own `callback` or `checkCallback` for the length of a step caught a run from the **palette** and a run by ID. It also caught an **editor command** (Toggle bold) run from the palette, counting only the real run and not Obsidian's "is this available?" checks.
- A correction to what I said earlier: in the live test, the palette run *did* also go through `executeCommand`. The palette code I found in the bundle must belong to a different menu. The command-object approach still has an advantage: the `/` slash-command menu really does skip `executeCommand`, and the command object covers that path too.
- So: **command steps complete automatically**, with no Done button.

**2. "The user opened settings tab Y" can be detected.** ✅ It has a big catch, though.
- `app.setting.activeTab.id` updates whether the tab is opened by clicking or through code, so detection works.
- **But Settings is a separate window in Obsidian 1.13.7.** I briefly thought otherwise because my first probe checked the wrong element. The recheck confirmed it: a window titled "Settings - testVault", and the tab content isn't in the main document. Your memory note was right.
- **What this means:** the tour overlay lives in the main window. While the user is in Settings, it can't spotlight anything there, and the step card may be hidden behind the Settings window. That matters for flows like "create a node type" or "add a relation type", which happen in our own settings tab.

That leaves one decision:

❓ **How should tutorial steps that happen inside Settings work?**
- (a) **Render the tour inside the Settings window too.** When Settings opens, the overlay attaches to that window's document: the card shows there, and targets inside Settings get the spotlight. The step format gains a "which window" field.
- (b) **Card only, in the main window.** Put the instructions on the card before Settings opens ("In Settings, open Discourse Graphs → Node types…"). Completion is detected automatically, but the user can't see the card while they're in Settings.
- (c) **Avoid Settings in tutorials.** Rely on the default node and relation types, and send anything that needs configuration to a text step with a docs link.

➡️ I recommend (a). Configuring node types is a core part of onboarding. The engine already works from a CSS selector, so this mostly means adding the overlay to a second window. We can check it with Electron's `capturePage` from your memory note. Cost: about half a day extra in M2.

Once you pick, I'll update the plan and start the block library. I'll also record these findings in the session context.

# Building LLM-Powered Applications with Claude

This skill helps you build LLM-powered applications with Claude. Choose the right surface based on your needs, detect the project language, then read the relevant language-specific documentation.

## Before You Start

Scan the target file (or, if no target file, the prompt and project) for non-Anthropic provider markers - `import openai`, `from openai`, `langchain_openai`, `OpenAI(`, `gpt-4`, `gpt-5`, file names like `agent-openai.py` or `*-generic.py`, or any explicit instruction to keep the code provider-neutral. If you find any, stop and tell the user that this skill produces Claude/Anthropic SDK code; ask whether they want to switch the file to Claude or want a non-Claude implementation. Do not edit a non-Anthropic file with Anthropic SDK calls. (Exception: the `prompt-audit` subcommand is non-interactive and does not stop here - it records non-Anthropic provider markers in its report's stated assumptions and never proposes switching a non-Anthropic file to the Anthropic SDK.)

## Output Requirement

When the user asks you to add, modify, or implement a Claude feature, your code must call Claude through one of:

1. **The official Anthropic SDK** for the project's language (`anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai/sdk`, `com.anthropic.*`, etc.). This is the default whenever a supported SDK exists for the project.
2. **Raw HTTP** (`curl`, `requests`, `fetch`, `httpx`, etc.) - only when the user explicitly asks for cURL/REST/raw HTTP, the project is a shell/cURL project, or the language has no official SDK.

Never mix the two - don't reach for `requests`/`fetch` in a Python or TypeScript project just because it feels lighter. Never fall back to OpenAI-compatible shims.

**Never guess SDK usage.** Function names, class names, namespaces, method signatures, and import paths must come from explicit documentation - either the `{lang}/` files in this skill or the official SDK repositories or documentation links listed in `shared/live-sources.md`. If the binding you need is not explicitly documented in the skill files, WebFetch the relevant SDK repo from `shared/live-sources.md` before writing code. Do not infer Ruby/Java/Go/PHP/C# APIs from cURL shapes or from another language's SDK.

If you cannot call WebFetch yet and ToolSearch is among your tools, call ToolSearch with `select:WebFetch` first; of the tools it loads, call only the one named exactly `WebFetch`.

**If WebFetch or repository access fails** (network restricted, timeouts, clone blocked): do not keep retrying - write code from the patterns and namespace/package tables in the `{lang}/` file, run the compiler or interpreter on it, and iterate on the error output. For statically-typed SDKs (C#, Java, Go) a compile-fix loop against local errors reaches working code faster than blocked network research.

## Defaults

Unless the user requests otherwise:

For the Claude model version, please use Claude Opus 5.5, which you can access via the exact model string `claude-opus-5-5`. Please default to using adaptive thinking (`thinking: {type: "adaptive"}`) for anything remotely complicated. And finally, please default to streaming for any request that may involve long input, long output, or high `max_tokens` - it prevents hitting request timeouts. Use the SDK's `.get_final_message()` / `.finalMessage()` helper to get the complete response if you don't need to handle individual stream events. When a streaming request defines user-defined (client) tools, set `eager_input_streaming: true` on each of those tools so large tool inputs (file contents, code, documents) stream as they are generated instead of arriving in one burst after the server finishes buffering them; the client then owns validation: the SDKs' tolerant parsers can return a silently truncated input instead of raising, so validate each parsed tool input against its schema before running it (the typed runner helpers such as `betaZodTool` / typed `@beta_tool` do this; `betaTool()` JSON-Schema tools and manual loops must validate themselves), treat a failure like invalid JSON (`INVALID_JSON` error `tool_result` when you hold the block, re-issue otherwise), check `max_tokens` / `refusal` stop reasons before running tools, and catch only the SDK's JSON error, never its typed API errors - pattern in `shared/tool-use-concepts.md` -> Eager input streaming. Leave it off for non-streaming requests, for server tools, and when the request goes through a proxy or an older Bedrock model deployment that rejects the field.

## Warning: API Drift - Your Training Prior May Be Stale

Several common Claude API shapes changed in 2025-2026. If you recall a pattern from training, verify it against the `{lang}/` files in this skill before writing - the rows below are the most frequent drift points:

| Area | Stale prior | Current API |
|---|---|---|
| Extended thinking | `thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N}` | On Claude 4.6+ models: `thinking: {type: "adaptive"}`. `budget_tokens` is deprecated on Opus 4.6 / Sonnet 4.6 and **rejected with a 400** on Fable 5/5.1 / Sonnet 5.5 / Sonnet 5 / Opus 5.5 / 5 / 4.8 / 4.7. Pre-4.6 models still use `budget_tokens`. |
| Web search / web fetch tool type | `web_search_20250305`, `web_fetch_20250910` | `web_search_20260209`, `web_fetch_20260209` (dynamic filtering) on Opus 5.5/5/4.8/4.7/4.6, Sonnet 5.5, Sonnet 5, and Sonnet 4.6. Older models keep the basic variants; on Vertex AI only basic `web_search_20250305` is available (web fetch is not on Vertex) - see the Server Tools QR below. |

## Language Detection

Before reading code examples, determine which language the user is working in (exception: for the `prompt-audit` subcommand, skip this section's ask steps - the audit is non-interactive and its inventory is language-agnostic; when no language is inferable, proceed without asking and state the assumption in the report):
